acts.title: Four tins and a lawyer
text: A couple walking on their own land found eight rusted tins that turned out to be extremely ___.
The coins inside were ___ to be worth around ten million dollars.
Their ___ was strong, because the tins were on their property and nobody else had ever mentioned them.
They had to hand everything over to an ___ while the decision was made.
A young man in another country ___ in a bag of diamonds the same week, and was given a reward.

items.q: In most countries it is ___ to keep lost property if you can find the owner.
The thieves left the paintings on the train, perhaps fearing ___.
He bought them at an ___ of property left on Italian trains.
A scrap metal ___ paid thirteen thousand dollars for the egg.
Without enough ___ places, we cannot protect the most vulnerable.
The campaign is trying to reduce street ___.
The two paintings turned out to be ___ thirty million euros.
New government plans may put thousands of people into ___.

tts: A scrap metal dealer who bought an antique gold egg for thirteen thousand dollars has made a profit of more than thirty-two million, after discovering that the egg was in fact one of the famous Russian Fabergé eggs. He had planned to sell it for the value of its gold and jewels, but when he researched it online he found a report about the eight Fabergé eggs still missing.

A Californian couple out for a walk around their property have accidentally found eight old tin cans full of gold coins. It is estimated that the coins are worth around ten million dollars. Their claim to ownership is strong, as the coins were found on their property, but they have still had to hand the coins over to an official while a decision is made.

An Italian car worker has discovered that two paintings hanging in his kitchen are worth around thirty million euros. They had been stolen from a house in London in 1970, and he bought them at an auction of lost property left on Italian trains. The police suspect that the thieves must have abandoned them on the train, perhaps fearing arrest.

A bag containing two hundred thousand dollars’ worth of diamonds found on the street has been returned to its owner. The dealer had dropped the bag on the way to have the diamonds polished, and did not expect to see them again. A young man handed them in to the police, and has received a reward.

items.q: What do the four stories have in common?
o: Somebody found something valuable that was not theirs
They all took place in Italy

items.q: How did the scrap metal dealer find out what the egg was?
What happened to the bag of diamonds?
o: A young man handed it in and was rewarded

tts: The scrap metal dealer paid thirteen thousand dollars and made a profit of more than thirty-two million.

The Californian couple found eight tin cans on their own property. The coins are estimated at around ten million dollars, and their claim to ownership is strong. Even so, they have had to hand the coins over to an official while a decision is made about who they actually belong to.

The two paintings were stolen from a house in London in 1970. The car worker bought them in 1974 at an auction of lost property left on Italian trains. The police suspect the thieves must have abandoned them, perhaps fearing arrest.
The diamond dealer had dropped the bag while taking the diamonds to be polished.

items.s: The scrap metal dealer originally planned to sell the egg for its gold and jewels.
The Californian couple found the coins on somebody else’s land.
The couple were allowed to keep the coins immediately.
The paintings were stolen in London before the car worker bought them.
The police think the thieves left the paintings on the train deliberately.
The diamond dealer expected to get his bag back.

tts: They have still had to hand the coins over to an official.
In most countries it is illegal to keep lost property unless you cannot find the owner.
You must report anything you find that is worth more than a certain amount.
You needn’t report a coin you pick up in the street.
You should hand it in, even if nobody would ever know.
You can’t simply keep something that clearly belongs to somebody else.

items.q: “They have had to hand the coins over.” Which idea is this?
o: Obligation coming from outside — the law

items.q: “You needn’t report a coin.” What does needn’t mean here?
“You can’t simply keep it.” What does can’t mean here?
Which of these is advice rather than obligation?
o: You have to hand it over.

acts.title: Present modals: how strong, and where the pressure comes from
rule: English does not have one word for “necessary”. It has several, and they differ in two ways: how strong the pressure is, and whether it comes from the speaker or from outside — a law, a timetable, a rule somebody else wrote.
points: Strong obligation, usually from the speaker. In writing it is also the standard form for rules and notices.
Strong obligation from outside the speaker: the law, the boss, the situation. This is the everyday spoken choice.
These are opposites, not variants. mustn’t = it is forbidden. don’t have to = it is not necessary.
Means exactly what don’t have to means. Slightly more formal, and more common in British English.
Advice or expectation, not obligation. Much weaker than must.
Two jobs: no permission (You can’t park here) and, in Lesson 6, no possibility.
eg: You must report anything valuable that you find.
Rule, stated by the speaker.
I have to hand it over to an official first.
Obligation from outside — the law says so.
You mustn’t keep it. That is theft.
Forbidden.
You don’t have to keep the receipt.
Not necessary — your choice.
You needn’t report a coin you find in the street.
Same meaning as don’t have to.
You should hand it in, even if nobody would know.
Advice, and a moral one.
You can’t park in front of the entrance.
No permission.
Do you have to work on Saturdays?
The normal question form. must has no do form.
I had to hand it over.
must has no past — had to fills the gap.
Staff are not allowed to leave the building at lunchtime.
be allowed to, the passive-sounding rule form.
acts.careful: “You mustn’t wear a tie” means it is banned. If you mean it is optional, you need “You don’t have to wear a tie.” This single pair causes more misunderstanding than any other modal at B2.

write.q: Write the rules on found property for somebody who has just moved to your country, in about 150 words. Use must or have to at least twice, mustn’t or aren’t allowed to at least once, and don’t have to or needn’t at least once. Make the difference between the last two unmistakable.
plan: what you are not allowed to do
write.model:
If you find something valuable here, you have to hand it in at a police station, and you have to do it within a reasonable time. That part is not a matter of opinion; it is the law, and the police will tell you the same.

You aren’t allowed to keep an item simply because nobody has claimed it. Ownership passes to the finder only after a fixed period, and only if the owner cannot be traced.

You don’t have to hand in a coin you pick up in the street, and nobody expects you to. You needn’t report anything below a small value at all.

Everything in between depends on the circumstances. A wallet with a driving licence in it must go in. An umbrella on a bus probably need not. The honest test is whether you could find the owner if you tried.
